land.text: Xichuan (Chengdu, taken 891) and Dongchuan (taken 897), Shannan West (Xingyuan, 902) and the Jingnan prefectures of Kui, Zhong, Wan and En (903), all won by Wang Jian as a Tang governor before he took the imperial title

predecessors.note: Wang Jian ruled these circuits under the Tang (Prince of Shu in 903) and declared the new state of Shu on 3 November 907 (Wang Jian page infobox).

land.text: Sichuan, western Hubei and parts of southern Gansu and Shaanxi, taken by the Later Tang in 925

successors.note: Sichuan broke away again as the Later Shu (934/935), which holds 'roughly the same territory' (Five Dynasties page); Cliopatria has Later Shu from 936.

rulers.name: Wang Yan (Wang Zongyan)
rulers.note: The Former Shu table calls him Wang Zongyan, its infobox Wang Yan; no temple name; the Wang Jian page gives 18 May 926 as his death.

correction.text: Cliopatria's Former Shu shape without Qin Prefecture (Tianshui) and the Baoji-Fengxiang country, which Qi held until 915-916

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 907-910 (Cliopatria starts the Former Shu in 911). Wang Jian's circuits were all in hand by 903; Qi still held Qin Prefecture and the Baoji-Fengxiang country ('In fall 915, Wang Jian launched a major attack against Qi. Feng Prefecture fell, and Li Jichong surrendered Qin'), so they are cut from Cliopatria's shape. The page names the prefectures, not a modern boundary: Qin is read as the Tianshui country, Fengxiang as Baoji.

correction.text: Cliopatria's Former Shu shape without Qin Prefecture (Tianshui) and the Baoji-Fengxiang country, which Qi held until 915-916

keyframe_review.note: Valid 911-914 with the correction; Cliopatria's shape (605,241 km2, identical to its 922 shape) already contains Tianshui and Baoji from 911, but the Wang Jian page dates their fall to 915 and 916. No page gives an infobox area; the Former Shu page gives none either. The Guizhou (22 percent of the province) and Yunnan fringes of the shape are not named by any opened page (the Five Dynasties page lists 'most of Sichuan, western Hubei, and parts of southern Gansu and Shaanxi'); left as unverified, not removed.

union.text: Qin Prefecture (Tianxiong's seat), surrendered to Shu by Li Jichong in fall 915

correction.text: Cliopatria's Former Shu shape without the Baoji-Fengxiang country, still Qi's in 915 (Qin and Feng prefectures taken that autumn); with all of Qin Prefecture (the Tianshui country), part of which Cliopatria draws inside its Qi shape rather than Shu's (reviewer ea-04-c)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 915: Feng and Qin prefectures taken from Qi in autumn 915 (Tianshui country inside); Fengxiang and Baoji still Qi's until autumn 916.

minus.text: Fengxiang and its surroundings, Qi's last ground

union.text: Qin Prefecture (Tianxiong's seat), surrendered to Shu by Li Jichong in fall 915

correction.text: Cliopatria's Former Shu shape without Fengxiang and its immediate surroundings, where Qi survived; Baoji taken in autumn 916; with all of Qin Prefecture (the Tianshui country), part of which Cliopatria draws inside its Qi shape rather than Shu's (reviewer ea-04-c)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 916-921: 'In fall 916, Wang Jian prepared another major attack against Qi' and Baoji was captured; Fengxiang held out ('The siege, however, was hampered by snowstorms, and Wang Jian decided to lift the siege'). Baoji is kept in Shu's hands here because the page does not return it; Fengxiang itself stays Qi's.

minus.text: Fengxiang and its surroundings, Qi's last ground

union.text: Qin Prefecture (Tianxiong's seat), surrendered to Shu by Li Jichong in fall 915

correction.text: Cliopatria's Former Shu shape without Fengxiang and its immediate surroundings, where Qi survived; Baoji taken in autumn 916; with all of Qin Prefecture (the Tianshui country), part of which Cliopatria draws inside its Qi shape rather than Shu's (reviewer ea-04-c)

keyframe_review.note: Valid 922-925 with the correction (same as 916-921); Cliopatria's shape is unchanged from 911. The state fell in 925 ('Fell in 925 when Wang's son surrendered to an advancing Later Tang army'), not later; the 925 end year matches Cliopatria.

region.text: Xichuan and Dongchuan around Chengdu, the core Wang Jian had held since 891-897

ledger.note: 907: Wang Jian proclaims the Great Shu at Chengdu. 'Wang thereafter declared himself emperor of a new state of Shu'; infobox reign 'November 3, 907 - July 11, 918'. The Former Shu page dates a 'Foundation of the State of Shu under Tang rule' to 903 (when he became Prince of Shu); the state proper starts with the imperial title. The page names circuits, not a boundary.

region.text: Qin Prefecture, Tianxiong's seat; Feng Prefecture is named by the page but not located

ledger.note: 915: Shu takes Qin and Feng prefectures from Qi. 'In fall 915, Wang Jian launched a major attack against Qi. Feng Prefecture fell, and Li Jichong surrendered Qin.' The page does not locate either prefecture; Qin is read as the Tianshui country, Feng is not placed.

region.text: Fengxiang, Qi's capital, besieged; Baoji captured

ledger.note: 916: Shu storms Baoji and besieges Fengxiang. 'In fall 916, Wang Jian prepared another major attack against Qi'; Baoji was captured and Fengxiang besieged.

region.text: Baoji, captured in the autumn 916 offensive

ledger.note: 916: Baoji falls to Shu. The page says Baoji was captured and does not say it was given back when the siege was lifted, so it stays Shu's here (a reading).

region.text: Fengxiang, where the siege was lifted

ledger.note: 916: Shu lifts the siege of Fengxiang. 'The siege, however, was hampered by snowstorms, and Wang Jian decided to lift the siege.' Fengxiang stays Qi's.

916: Wang Jian renames the state Han. 'He then declared a change of the state's name from Shu to Han' (fall 916); the Former Shu page says 917-918 and lists the era Tianhan for 917. Not the Southern Han, which is a separate state.
918: the state takes the name Shu again, in Wang Jian's last year. 'In early spring 918, Wang Jian changed the name of the state from Han back to Shu.' He died 11 July 918 and Wang Yan succeeded.

region.text: most of Sichuan, western Hubei and parts of southern Gansu and Shaanxi

ledger.note: 925: Later Tang takes Sichuan. 'Fell in 925 when Wang's son surrendered to an advancing Later Tang army' (Wang Yan, Wang Jian's son); the page lists the realm as 'most of Sichuan, western Hubei, and parts of southern Gansu and Shaanxi'. No month or campaign dates on any opened page.

region.text: the Great Shu, ended by the Later Tang

ledger.note: 925: the Former Shu ends. Infobox 'Ended by the Later Tang: 925'; last era name Xiankang (925). The land passes to the Later Tang; Sichuan is independent again as the Later Shu from 934/935.

wars.name: Shu-Qi war

zones.text: Baoji, captured 916; Fengxiang besieged and relieved

wars.outcome: Shu victory on the Qin and Feng prefectures (autumn 915) and Baoji (autumn 916); the Fengxiang siege was lifted, leaving Qi a rump around its capital.
wars.note: 'In 911, though, the Shu-Qi alliance would break up over marital relations.' Late in 911 'Shu forces were able to decisively defeat Qi forces, forcing them to withdraw'. Li Maozhen had asked in 910 for the cession of Ba and Jian prefectures; Wang refused.

wars.name: Joint Shu-Qi attack on Chang'an
wars.outcome: Failed: the allied armies withdrew ('Qi forces were defeated by Liu Zhijun at Mu Valley'); no border moved.
wars.note: The Wang Jian page says 'the Former Shu and Jin forces withdrew'; the Li Maozhen page names Qi, which is the reading used here.

wars.name: Later Tang conquest of Former Shu

zones.text: Sichuan and the lands round it

wars.outcome: Later Tang victory: 'When the main Later Tang forces under Li Jiji arrived at Chengdu, Wang Yan formally surrendered'; the Former Shu ended in 925 and Wang Yan and his family were executed in 926.
wars.note: 'By fall 925, Later Tang was deep in the preparation of an invasion of Former Shu'; Emperor Zhuangzong named 'his son Li Jiji the Prince of Wei' titular commander with Guo Chongtao in actual command; Wuxing Circuit and Wude Circuit (Mianyang) commanders surrendered, and Wang Zongbi seized the Chengdu palace and offered to surrender. No month is on any opened page for the invasion or the surrender; the Five Dynasties page has 'Fell in 925 when Wang's son surrendered'.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line is on any opened page. The northern frontier with Qi on the Qin-Feng-Baoji country moved in 915 and 916 and is drawn from prefecture names; the western and southern fringes (Guizhou, Yunnan) are approximate.

sources.title: Former Shu
sources.note: Identity, capital, rulers, 903 foundation under Tang rule, 'Ended by the Later Tang: 925', the Han name. A thin page: no area, no wars.

sources.title: Wang Jian (Former Shu)
sources.note: The circuits won 891-903, the 3 November 907 accession, the Shu-Qi war 908-916 (Qin and Feng 915, Baoji 916), the Shu-Han-Shu renaming. Silent on 925.

sources.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period
sources.note: Former Shu extent ('most of Sichuan, western Hubei, and parts of southern Gansu and Shaanxi') and the 925 fall to the Later Tang; also Later Shu as the same territory.

sources.title: Li Maozhen
sources.note: Qi's side of the 908 failed attack and the 911 break with Shu.

sources.title: Wang Yan (Former Shu)
sources.note: The 925 Later Tang invasion: commanders Li Jiji and Guo Chongtao, surrender at Chengdu (no month), Wang Yan's execution in spring 926 and the circuits of 924-925.

sources.title: Later Tang
sources.note: Opened for the 925 conquest; thin and silent on Shu, Qi and Wang Yan (gives only May 923 as the founding and 11 January 937 as the end).

notes: Pages opened on 2026-10-19: Former Shu, Wang Jian, Wang Yan, Li Maozhen, Later Tang and the shared Five Dynasties page. The Former Shu and Later Tang pages are thin and the Wang Yan page gives no month, so the 925 conquest has no month (confidence 3 on the year and the conqueror only). Cliopatria's two Former Shu shapes (911-921, 922-925) are the same outline, 605,241 km2; it covers 98 percent of Chongqing, 66 percent of Sichuan, 38 percent of Shaanxi, 13 percent of Gansu, 12 percent of Hubei, and fringes of Guizhou and Yunnan. No page gives an infobox area, so no area ratio was possible. The Cliopatria shape places Baoji (Fengxiang's neighbour) and 69 percent of the Tianshui country inside Shu from 911; the Wang Jian page dates their fall to 915-916, so keyframes 907, 911, 915, 916 and 922 cut them back. The Qi Kingdom shape in Cliopatria (Pingliang and Ningxia) leaves Fengxiang to nobody: see qi-kingdom. The Feng Prefecture of the 915 gain is not located by the page and is left out of the region. Wang Jian's earlier gains (Chengdu 891, Dongchuan 897, Hanzhong 902, the Jingnan prefectures 903) predate the state and are recorded in predecessors only. The Wang Jian page says the Han name began in fall 916; the Former Shu page says 917-918; the ledger follows the Wang Jian page. The Wang Yan page lists Tianxiong (Tianshui) among Shu's circuits in 924-925, consistent with the 915 gain. Pages say nothing on the Shu-Nanzhao frontier, the Shu-Southern Wu/Chu/Jingnan frontiers or the Tibetan frontier in 907-925; the neighbours list in the seed shows Chu, Later Liang, Qi and the Tibetans touching Shu.
